title: Packet Capture
sub: Record your own traffic with tcpdump and Wireshark, read it line by line, and filter it down to the packets you care about
goals: Capture and read your own traffic with tcpdump, including the handshake, DNS and ARP
Write BPF capture filters and display filters, and say which tool uses which
Decode a tcpdump line field by field: timestamp, endpoints, flags, sequence numbers, window, length
Save a capture to a .pcap file and analyze it later with tcpdump, tshark and Wireshark
Turn live or saved packets into counts and lists with grep, awk and tshark fields
Annotate a packet trace and explain what each packet is doing

blocks.text: Every tool so far reported what a program saw: `curl` told you the status code, `ping` told you the round trip, `nmap` told you the port state. A packet capture shows what actually crossed the wire, byte for byte, including the parts no tool summarizes: the SYN that never got an answer, the DNS query that fired twice, the retransmission that explains why a page took four seconds. When a network problem resists every higher-level tool, a capture settles the argument. In this chapter you will capture the traffic of your own Mac, read it, save it, and filter it down to exactly the packets that matter.

A packet capture can contain passwords, session cookies, messages, the sites you visit and everything your devices send in the clear. **Capture only on your own Mac, your own network and your own devices.** Recording other people's traffic without permission is illegal in many jurisdictions (wiretapping and computer-misuse laws), whether or not the network is "open". Do not capture on school, work or public Wi-Fi except under written policy or permission. Treat every `.pcap` file you make as a secret: do not post it, attach it to a bug report, or leave it in a synced folder before you have looked at what is inside.
Why capture, and what it can and cannot see

A capture tool asks the kernel for a copy of every frame that crosses a network interface, before or after the normal protocol stack handles it. Nothing is modified and the traffic is not slowed. It is the closest thing a network has to a flight recorder.
Reach for a capture when:

items.text: a connection is slow or hangs and you need to see **which** step takes the time (DNS, handshake, server reply);
two machines disagree about what was sent, and you want evidence from one side;
you need to confirm that a firewall rule, a VPN or a NAT really does what you think;
you are learning a protocol and want to see it rather than read about it.

blocks.text: What a capture cannot do: it cannot read **encrypted** payloads. For an `https` request you will see the DNS lookup, the TCP handshake, the TLS `ClientHello` (with the server name in plain text, the SNI from [HTTP and TLS](#http)), then opaque encrypted records, with sizes and timing. That is still enough to diagnose most problems. On Wi-Fi you also see only **your own** traffic plus broadcast and multicast frames, because every client has its own encryption keys. That is the design working as intended.

The widget shows the nesting you will see in every capture. The frame carries an Ethernet header (MAC addresses), which carries an IP header (addresses, TTL, protocol number), which carries a TCP or UDP header (ports, flags, sequence numbers), which carries the application data. Each tool in this chapter can show you any of those layers.
Permissions, interfaces and the first capture

Capturing needs access to the kernel's **BPF** (Berkeley Packet Filter) devices, `/dev/bpf0` and friends, which only root can open by default. So `tcpdump` needs `sudo`. Wireshark's installer adds a helper (ChmodBPF) that lets members of an admin-style group capture without `sudo`; see the Wireshark section below.
First find out which interface carries your traffic. The local-network chapter ([net-local](#net-local)) showed `route -n get default`, and `networksetup -listallhardwareports` maps names to ports.

blocks.code:
route -n get default | awk '/interface:/ {print $2}'
sudo tcpdump -D

$ route -n get default | awk '/interface:/ {print $2}'
en0
$ sudo tcpdump -D
1.en0 [Up, Running, Wireless]
2.awdl0 [Up, Running, Wireless]
3.llw0 [Up, Running, Wireless]
4.utun0 [Up, Running]
5.bridge0 [Up, Running]
6.lo0 [Up, Running, Loopback]

blocks.text: `en0` is usually Wi-Fi on a laptop. `lo0` is loopback, where traffic between programs on your own Mac travels, so it is the perfect safe place to start: you generate every packet yourself. macOS has no `any` pseudo-interface, so choose one interface per capture.

macOS ships `/usr/sbin/tcpdump`, built by Apple with extensions. It supports the usual BPF filters plus `pktap`, a virtual interface that wraps others and tags each packet with the **process** that sent it (see the metadata section below). The Wi-Fi flag `-I` (monitor mode) exists but is for advanced 802.11 work and usually disconnects you while active; Apple's Wireless Diagnostics has a Sniffer for that job.

blocks.name: tcpdump
blocks.sum: Capture packets from a network interface, filter them with BPF expressions, print them or save them to a pcap file.
blocks.syntax: sudo tcpdump [-nn] [-i iface] [-c count] [-w file | -r file] [-A | -X] [-e] [-v] [-l] [-q] [-tttt] ['filter']

how.text: `tcpdump` opens a BPF device on one interface and asks the kernel for copies of the frames that match a **capture filter**. The filter runs inside the kernel, so unwanted packets never reach tcpdump: filtering at capture time is cheap and keeps files small. For each packet that passes, tcpdump prints one summary line, decoding as much of Ethernet, IP, TCP, UDP, ICMP, ARP and DNS as it can.

It prints to the terminal by default. With `-w file` it writes the raw packets to a **pcap** file instead (the format every analysis tool reads), and `-r file` reads one back. Print options such as `-A` or `-X` change how each packet is shown without changing what was captured. Stop with Control-C; tcpdump then prints how many packets it captured and how many the kernel dropped.

Always use `-n` (no host-name lookups) and usually `-nn` (also no port-name lookups). Otherwise tcpdump asks DNS for every address it prints, which slows output, creates extra DNS traffic and pollutes the capture it is showing you.

flags.d: Interface to capture on (`en0`, `lo0`). Required in practice on macOS.
List interfaces available for capture.
Do not resolve addresses to names.
Also do not translate port numbers to service names (`80`, not `http`).
Stop after N packets. Always set it while experimenting.
Write raw packets to FILE (pcap). Add `-U` to flush each packet as it arrives.
Read packets from a pcap file instead of the network. No `sudo` needed.
Print each packet's payload as ASCII (good for reading HTTP).
Print the payload in hex and ASCII. `-XX` includes the Ethernet header.
Print the link-level header (MAC addresses).
More protocol detail (TTL, IP id, checksums, full DNS answers).
Quiet: shorter lines with less protocol information.
Line-buffer output so a pipe sees lines at once (use with `grep`, `awk`).
Print a full date and time on every line. `-tt` prints Unix epoch seconds, handy for arithmetic.
Bytes to capture per packet. Modern tcpdump captures whole packets by default; `-s 0` is the old way to ask for that.
Rotate output files every MB million bytes, keeping N files (`-w` required).
Apple extension: print packet metadata such as the process name (use with `-i pktap,en0`).

gotchas: Without `-c` or a Control-C, tcpdump runs forever, and `-w` files grow until the disk is full. Use `-c`, or rotate with `-C` and `-W`.
Run with `sudo` and the output file belongs to root. Fix with `sudo chown $USER trace.pcap`, or you will get `Permission denied` when you open it in Wireshark.
A filter with brackets or parentheses must be in quotes in zsh: `tcp[tcpflags]` unquoted fails with `zsh: no matches found`. Prefer one quoted string for the whole filter.
"0 packets captured" almost always means the wrong interface (`en1` instead of `en0`), a filter that matches nothing, or no traffic yet. Check with `-D` and try without a filter.
notes: tcpdump writes its status lines (`listening on en0, link-type EN10MB`, and the final packet counts) to stderr, so `2> /dev/null` keeps them out of a pipeline.

blocks.text: Your first capture: a TCP connection on loopback
You generate every packet, so nothing private is involved. Use two tabs. In tab one start the practice server from [HTTP and TLS](#http):

blocks.code: cd ~/lab && python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1

blocks.text: In tab two start the capture on the loopback interface, filtering for that one port, and stop after 12 packets:

blocks.code: sudo tcpdump -nn -i lo0 -c 12 'tcp port 8000'

blocks.text: In tab three fetch a file:

blocks.code: curl -s -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:8000/README.txt

blocks.text: The capture prints something like this (shortened; the options differ on your Mac):

You can read the entire conversation from these twelve lines. Lines 1 to 3 are the **three-way handshake**. Line 4 is the HTTP request (87 bytes of payload) and line 5 its acknowledgement. Lines 6 and 8 carry the response headers and the file (165 + 214 bytes), acknowledged by lines 7 and 10. Lines 9, 11 and 12 close the connection: the server sent its FIN first because `http.server` replies in HTTP/1.0 and hangs up when it is done. Compare it to the animation in the handshake widget:
Reading one line field by field
Here is the SYN again, one token at a time. After this anatomy you can read any TCP line from any capture.

tokens.exp: timestamp: hours, minutes, seconds and microseconds, local time
the network protocol of this packet (IPv4)
source address and port: the client, an ephemeral port
destination address and port: the server
TCP flags: S is SYN, the first packet of a connection
sequence number: the byte number this segment starts at (absolute only on a SYN)
receive window: how many bytes the sender is willing to receive right now
TCP options: largest segment, window scaling, selective ACK
payload bytes in this packet (a SYN carries none)

blocks.text: The **flags** deserve a table, because they tell the state of the conversation at a glance. A trailing dot means the ACK flag is set.

head: tcpdump shows
Flags set
Meaning
rows: acknowledgement, no data (third packet and every pure acknowledgement)
data, deliver it now; most request and response packets
reset: refuse or abort the connection

blocks.text: Three number fields need one more sentence each. `seq A:B` means this segment carries bytes A up to (not including) B of the stream, relative to the start (tcpdump prints **relative** numbers after the first packet; `-S` turns that off and shows absolute ones). `ack N` means "I have received everything before byte N; send N next". `win` is the receiver's window; after the handshake it is multiplied by the scale factor the two sides agreed in `wscale` (the window in a SYN itself is never scaled). In a healthy flow `length` of one side's packet plus its `seq` equals the other side's next `ack`: line 4 carried bytes 1 up to 88, and line 5 answered `ack 88`.

Run the capture above. Find the three lines of the handshake. Subtract the time of the SYN from the time of the SYN+ACK: on loopback it is under a millisecond. On a capture to a real server (next section), the same subtraction is the **round-trip time**, the number `ping` reports, measured by TCP itself.
Capturing the payload
`-A` prints each payload as text. This is how you read unencrypted HTTP with your own eyes, and why plain `http` should never carry anything secret:
The first line of garbage characters is the IP and TCP headers rendered as ASCII; the readable text after it is the HTTP message. For hex plus ASCII side by side use `-X`.
Capture filters: BPF

The quoted expression at the end of the command is a **BPF filter** (Berkeley Packet Filter). It is compiled and runs in the kernel, so only matching packets are copied up. The language is small. Learn the primitives and combine them with `and`, `or`, `not` and parentheses.

head: Primitive
Matches
Example
rows: packets to or from address A
TCP or UDP port P, either direction
TCP packets with the SYN flag

blocks.text: Combine them:

blocks.code:
sudo tcpdump -nn -i en0 'host 192.168.1.50 and port 22'
sudo tcpdump -nn -i en0 'udp port 53 or tcp port 53'
sudo tcpdump -nn -i en0 'net 192.168.1.0/24 and not port 22'
sudo tcpdump -nn -i en0 'icmp or arp'

blocks.text: Quote the whole expression. In zsh `(`, `)`, `[`, `]`, `&` and `!` are special characters, and without quotes they never reach tcpdump.
Matching TCP flags
The TCP header has a byte of flag bits, and BPF can read it as `tcp[tcpflags]`. Combined with the names `tcp-syn`, `tcp-ack`, `tcp-fin`, `tcp-rst` and `tcp-push`, you can pick out specific packets:

head: Goal
Filter
rows: New connection attempts only (SYN, no ACK)

blocks.title: A BPF filter that finds new connection attempts

tokens.exp: read the flags byte of the TCP header
bitwise AND: keep only the bits we name
the two bits to look at: SYN and ACK
of those two bits, only SYN is set (a SYN, not a SYN+ACK)

blocks.text: The pattern is: mask the byte with `&`, then compare. `(tcp-syn|tcp-ack) == tcp-syn` reads "of the SYN and ACK bits, only SYN is set". To find connection attempts that were **refused**, filter for resets and look at which port they come from. That is exactly how a scanner learns a port is closed, and how you recognise a scan in your own captures.

blocks.name: tcpdump filters
blocks.sum: A cookbook of BPF capture filters for the questions you ask most often.

how.text: The filter is a boolean expression over header fields. Primitives are joined with `and`, `or`, `not`, and grouped with parentheses. `host`, `net` and `port` without a direction match either end. Qualifiers like `src` and `dst` narrow to one end. A filter is compiled when tcpdump starts, so a syntax error appears immediately as `tcpdump: syntax error in filter expression`.

Capture filters differ from Wireshark **display filters**: they use a different, older syntax, and they decide what is recorded, while display filters decide what is shown from what was already recorded. Mixing the two syntaxes is the most common beginner error (see the table later in the chapter).

Only web traffic that is not to your own server
examples.code: sudo tcpdump -nn -i en0 'tcp port 443 and not host {{labhost}}'

gotchas: `host example.com` resolves the name once, when tcpdump starts. A site with several or changing addresses is only partly captured. Resolve and filter on IPs: `dig +short example.com`.
`port 53` matches either end, so it also matches *answers* coming from a server on port 53. Use `dst port 53` to see only queries.

blocks.text: Read a real conversation: DNS, then TCP, then HTTP

Now capture traffic that leaves your Mac. The goal is one command, `curl http://example.com`, and every packet it causes. Plain `http` is used on purpose, so the payload is readable. First, resolve the server address so that the filter can be specific, and warm nothing up: you want the DNS query to be visible.

blocks.code:
ip=$(dig +short example.com | head -1); echo $ip
sudo tcpdump -nn -tttt -i en0 -c 30 "host $ip or port 53"

blocks.text: While the capture waits, run `curl -s -o /dev/null http://example.com` in another tab. The filter is in double quotes so zsh expands `$ip`. Because `port 53` is in the filter, any other DNS your Mac does at the moment also appears; that is normal.

Read it as a story. Line 1: your Mac asks the router (`192.168.1.1`, port 53) for the address of `example.com`; the `+` means "recursion desired" and `A?` is the question. Line 2: the router answers with `A 93.184.216.34`, 11.8 ms later. Only after that does anything touch the web server: lines 3 to 5 are the handshake (the gap between the SYN and the SYN+ACK, 19.3 ms, is the round trip to the server), line 6 is the HTTP request, and line 8 begins the response. Notice that tcpdump names the application protocol (`HTTP: GET / HTTP/1.1`) for port 80.
This is the picture that `curl -w` condensed into numbers: `time_namelookup` was the first two lines, `time_connect` the handshake, `time_starttransfer` the wait before line 8.
Raw bytes: what -X shows

Sometimes the summary line is not enough, and you need the actual header bytes. The Python below parses the SYN packet from line 3, from the hex that `tcpdump -XX` or Wireshark would show. Run it, then change a byte and watch the field change.

blocks.code:
import struct
import ipaddress

hexdump = (
    "450000401c46400040060000c0a801175db8d822"   # IPv4 header, 20 bytes
    "cfe60050a78260e200000000b002ffff00000000"   # TCP header, 20 bytes
    "020405b4010303060101080a000dee7d0000000004020000"  # TCP options, 24 bytes
)
pkt = bytes.fromhex(hexdump)

ver_ihl, tos, total, ident, frag, ttl, proto, csum, src, dst = struct.unpack("!BBHHHBBH4s4s", pkt[:20])
ihl = (ver_ihl & 0x0F) * 4
sport, dport, seq, ack, off, flags, win, csum2, urg = struct.unpack("!HHIIBBHHH", pkt[ihl:ihl + 20])

names = {0x01: "FIN", 0x02: "SYN", 0x04: "RST", 0x08: "PSH", 0x10: "ACK"}
set_flags = [n for bit, n in names.items() if flags & bit]

print("IP  version", ver_ihl >> 4, "header", ihl, "bytes, total", total, "bytes, TTL", ttl, "proto", proto)
print("    ", ipaddress.ip_address(src), "->", ipaddress.ip_address(dst))
print("TCP port", sport, "->", dport, "flags", "+".join(set_flags), "seq", seq, "ack", ack)
print("    header", (off >> 4) * 4, "bytes, window", win, "payload", total - ihl - (off >> 4) * 4, "bytes")
blocks.out:
IP  version 4 header 20 bytes, total 64 bytes, TTL 64 proto 6
     192.168.1.23 -> 93.184.216.34
TCP port 53222 -> 80 flags SYN seq 2810339554 ack 0
    header 44 bytes, window 65535 payload 0 bytes

blocks.text: The first byte `45` is "version 4, header length 5 words of 4 bytes". `06` at offset 9 is the protocol number for TCP (17 is UDP, 1 is ICMP). The TCP header is 44 bytes, not 20, because of 24 bytes of options: the MSS, window scale, timestamps and SACK that tcpdump printed in brackets. You will write a parser like this against live sockets in [Python for networking](#py-net).
ARP: the local-network handshake

Before your Mac can send an IP packet to a device on the LAN, it needs that device's MAC address, and it learns it with **ARP** (Address Resolution Protocol). ARP is not IP; it rides directly on Ethernet, so a filter on `ip` would miss it. `-e` shows the MAC addresses involved. First look at the cache and then force one lookup:

blocks.code:
arp -an | grep 192.168.1.50
sudo arp -d 192.168.1.50
sudo tcpdump -nn -e -i en0 -c 2 arp

blocks.text: In another tab, `ping -c 1 192.168.1.50`. You will see the question and its answer:

blocks.code:
$ sudo tcpdump -nn -e -i en0 -c 2 arp
09:56:12.301552 f0:18:98:3a:6d:21 > ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, ethertype ARP (0x0806), length 42: Request who-has 192.168.1.50 tell 192.168.1.23, length 28
09:56:12.304910 dc:a6:32:7e:41:b8 > f0:18:98:3a:6d:21, ethertype ARP (0x0806), length 60: Reply 192.168.1.50 is-at dc:a6:32:7e:41:b8, length 46

blocks.text: The request is sent to the **broadcast** MAC `ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff`, so every device hears "who has 192.168.1.50?". Only the owner replies, directly to your MAC (`f0:18:98:3a:6d:21`), with its own. Your Mac stores the pair in its ARP table for a few minutes, which is what `arp -an` shows.

blocks.title: sudo arp -d is safe here, but read it first

blocks.text: `sudo arp -d IP` deletes one entry from your ARP cache; the Mac simply asks again at the next packet. Delete only the single address you name. Do not use `arp -d -a` while connected to something important: it flushes every entry and briefly interrupts local connections.
Saving captures and analyzing them later

Reading live packets is hard because they scroll. Capture to a file, then analyze it as many times as you like, with `sudo` only for the capture. This is also how you take a capture on one machine (a Pi) and study it on another.

blocks.code:
sudo tcpdump -nn -i en0 -c 500 -w trace.pcap 'not port 22'
sudo chown $USER trace.pcap
tcpdump -nn -r trace.pcap | head
ls -l trace.pcap

blocks.text: Excluding your own SSH session (`not port 22`) matters when you capture on a machine you are logged into over SSH: otherwise your terminal output travels over the connection you are capturing, which produces more packets, which are printed... until the capture is all noise.

The file is in pcap format. Wireshark opens it by double-click, `tcpdump -r` and `tshark -r` read it, and `capinfos trace.pcap` (installed with Wireshark) summarises it: packet count, duration, data rate. `editcap -c 1000 trace.pcap part.pcap` splits a big file into pieces of 1000 packets, and `mergecap` joins files.
When you must leave a capture running for hours, use rotation instead of one huge file:

blocks.code: sudo tcpdump -nn -i en0 -w ring.pcap -C 10 -W 5 'port 53'

blocks.text: That keeps five files of about 10 MB each and overwrites the oldest. Stop with Control-C.
Wireshark and tshark

`tcpdump` is the right tool for a quick look and for remote machines. For serious reading you want **Wireshark**: the same capture engine with a graphical interface that decodes thousands of protocols, colors by type, and lets you click a packet and see every field. **tshark** is its command-line twin, built for pipes.

blocks.code: brew install --cask wireshark-app

blocks.text: The Homebrew cask is called `wireshark-app` (older instructions say `wireshark`; if one name is not found, try the other with `brew search wireshark`). It installs `Wireshark.app` in `/Applications`, symlinks the command-line tools `tshark`, `dumpcap`, `capinfos`, `editcap` and `mergecap` into `/opt/homebrew/bin`, and runs two installers: **ChmodBPF**, which gives your admin account permission to capture without `sudo`, and one that adds Wireshark to the path. Enter your password when asked, and log out and back in (or reboot) if capturing says "permission denied". Do not also install the separate `wireshark-chmodbpf` cask; the two conflict. The plain `wireshark` formula is a command-line-only build and conflicts with the app.
A tour of the Wireshark window
Open Wireshark and double-click `en0` (or `lo0` for loopback) to start capturing; the toolbar's red square stops it. The window has three panes you read top to bottom:

items.text: **Packet list** (top): one row per packet with number, time, source, destination, protocol and a summary. Colors mark protocol types; black with red text marks problems such as resets and retransmissions.
**Packet details** (middle): the selected packet as a tree: Frame, Ethernet, Internet Protocol, TCP, the application. Click a line and the bytes it covers highlight in the bottom pane.
**Packet bytes** (bottom): hex and ASCII.

blocks.text: The **display filter bar** above the packet list decides which rows are shown. It is green when the filter is valid and red when it is not. Typing `tcp.` pops up every TCP field you can filter on, which is the fastest way to learn the field names.
Other features you will use daily:

items.text: **Follow a stream:** right-click a TCP packet, Follow, TCP Stream. Wireshark reassembles the whole conversation and shows the text of both directions in two colors. This is the quickest way to read an HTTP exchange or a banner.

**Statistics, Conversations:** lists every pair of endpoints with bytes and packets, so a top-talkers table is two clicks. **Protocol Hierarchy** shows the percentage of each protocol. **I/O Graphs** plots packets or bytes over time.
**Analyze, Expert Information:** lists retransmissions, resets, zero windows and other anomalies Wireshark spotted for you.
**Capture options:** choose the interface and type a **capture filter** (BPF syntax) before you start, to keep the file small.
**File, Export Specified Packets:** save just the packets you filtered.

blocks.text: Two filter languages

This is the single most confusing point for beginners, so it gets its own table. Wireshark uses **BPF** for capture filters (typed before capture, the same syntax as `tcpdump`) and its own **display filter** language for filtering what is shown.

head: You want
Capture filter (BPF: tcpdump's last argument / tshark `-f`)
Display filter (Wireshark / tshark `-Y`)

blocks.text: Capture filters are fast and limited because they run in the kernel before decoding. Display filters understand every decoded field but only work on what you already captured. Use a capture filter to keep the file manageable and display filters to ask questions of it.

blocks.name: tshark
blocks.sum: Wireshark's command-line packet analyzer: capture, decode, filter and print chosen fields, ready for pipes.
blocks.syntax: tshark [-i iface] [-f 'capture filter'] [-r file] [-Y 'display filter'] [-T fields -e field ...] [-c N] [-w file] [-q -z stat]

how.text: `tshark` uses the same capture library and the same decoders as Wireshark, so it understands the same protocols and the same display-filter language. Live capture uses `-i` and the BPF filter `-f`; reading a file uses `-r`. `-Y` applies a display filter, which is checked after decoding.

Its power for shell users is `-T fields`: you name the fields you want with `-e` and tshark prints them separated by tabs, one packet per line. Combined with `sort | uniq -c`, a question like "which names did my Mac look up?" becomes a one-liner. The `-z` option adds statistics tables such as per-second I/O, TCP conversations and HTTP request counts; use `-q` to suppress the packet lines so only the table prints.

anat.exp: display filter: DNS queries, not answers
print chosen fields instead of the packet summary
the field to print: the name asked about

gotchas: DNS answers repeat the query name, so counting `dns.qry.name` without `dns.flags.response == 0` doubles every count.

`-f` is a BPF capture filter and `-Y` is a display filter. A capture filter in `-Y` (`-Y 'port 53'`) is a syntax error, and a display filter in `-f` (`-f 'ip.addr == 192.168.1.50'`) is rejected as an invalid capture filter.
Live capture needs the same permissions as tcpdump. If `tshark -i en0` says "permission denied", the ChmodBPF installer has not taken effect yet (log out and in), or use `sudo`.
notes: Field names changed in Wireshark 3.x: TLS fields start with `tls.`, older tutorials use `ssl.`. List fields with `tshark -G fields | grep -i server_name`.

blocks.title: Why you can see which sites an HTTPS connection asked for

blocks.text: Capture a browser or `curl https://example.com` and run the SNI pipe above. The server name travels in the clear in the TLS ClientHello so the server knows which certificate to present ([HTTP and TLS](#http)). Everything after the handshake is encrypted, but the name, the size and the timing remain visible to anyone on the path. That is the real limit of "HTTPS hides what you do".

blocks.name: capinfos
blocks.sum: Print a summary of a capture file: packet count, duration, size and data rate.

how.text: `capinfos` reads the headers of a capture file and reports facts about it without decoding every packet: file type, number of packets, time of the first and last packet, capture duration, bytes and average rates. Run it first on a file somebody gave you, to learn how big and how long it is before you open it. It ships with Wireshark and works on pcap and pcapng.

flags.d: Show only the packet count.
Show only the capture duration in seconds.

examples.desc: Summarise a capture
Just the packet count as a number
examples.code: capinfos -c trace.pcap | awk -F: '/Number of packets/ {gsub(/ /, "", $2); print $2}'

gotchas: `-c` still prints a label before the number, which is why the pipe above extracts it with awk.

blocks.name: editcap
blocks.sum: Copy a capture file while cutting it: split into pieces, keep a packet range or a time window.
blocks.syntax: editcap [-c packets] [-r] [-A start -B stop] infile outfile [packet-range]

how.text: `editcap` reads one capture file and writes another, optionally dropping or splitting packets on the way. It never changes the captured bytes, so it is a safe way to trim a huge file to the 30 seconds that matter, or to cut a file into pieces small enough for Wireshark to open quickly. With `-c N` it writes a series of output files of N packets each, numbering them for you.

flags.d: Split into files of N packets each.
Keep (rather than delete) the listed packet ranges.
Keep only packets after / before a timestamp (`"2026-10-08 09:50:00"`).

examples.desc: Split a large capture into 1000-packet files
Keep only packets 100 to 200
Split, then count packets in each piece
examples.code: editcap -c 500 trace.pcap part.pcap && for f in part_*.pcap; do print "$f $(tcpdump -nn -r $f 2> /dev/null | wc -l)"; done

blocks.text: Which process sent that packet?

Apple added something classic tcpdump lacks: the kernel knows which process owns each socket, and the `pktap` pseudo-interface attaches that to every packet. Use `-k` to print it and `-Q` to filter on it. This answers the question a plain capture cannot: **which app is making this traffic?**

blocks.code: sudo tcpdump -q -nn -i pktap,en0 -k -c 10

$ sudo tcpdump -q -nn -i pktap,en0 -k -c 3
tcpdump: listening on pktap,en0, link-type PKTAP (Apple DLT_PKTAP), capture size 524288 bytes
(en0, proc curl:61288, svc BE, out) IP 192.168.1.23.53310 > 93.184.216.34.80: tcp 74
(en0, proc curl:61288, svc BE, in) IP 93.184.216.34.80 > 192.168.1.23.53310: tcp 1448
(en0, proc mDNSResponder:312, svc BE, out) IP 192.168.1.23.5353 > 224.0.0.251.5353: UDP, length 41

blocks.text: Each line begins with the interface, the process name and PID, the service class and the direction (`in` or `out`). The `-Q` option takes a metadata filter, for example `-Q 'proc =curl'` to keep only packets from processes named `curl`; the exact syntax is in the "PACKET METADATA FILTER" section of `man tcpdump` on your Mac. This is Apple-specific: on Linux or with tshark the same idea needs other tools.
Pipe recipes
The `-l` flag (line-buffered) is what lets a live capture feed a pipeline. Without it the output is buffered in blocks and your `awk` sees nothing for seconds.
**Top talkers by volume.** With `-q`, every TCP line ends in `tcp N` and every UDP line in `length N`, so the last field is the payload size. Sum it by source address:

blocks.code:
sudo tcpdump -nn -q -l -c 500 -i en0 'ip and (tcp or udp)' 2> /dev/null \
  | awk '{split($3, a, "."); ip = a[1] "." a[2] "." a[3] "." a[4]; bytes[ip] += $NF} END {for (i in bytes) print bytes[i], i}' \
  | sort -rn | head

blocks.text: The third field is `192.168.1.23.52814`: the address and the port joined by dots. Splitting on `.` and rejoining the first four pieces drops the port. IPv4 only; the `ip` in the filter keeps IPv6 lines out of the way.
**Count connection attempts** in a window of traffic:

blocks.code: sudo tcpdump -nn -l -c 200 -i en0 'tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn|tcp-ack) == tcp-syn' 2> /dev/null | wc -l

blocks.text: **Extract DNS query names** from a live capture. A query line contains a token such as `A? example.com.`, so `grep -o` can pull out just the question:

blocks.code: sudo tcpdump -nn -l -c 100 -i en0 'dst port 53' 2> /dev/null | grep -Eo '[A-Z0-9]+\? [^ ]+' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

$ sudo tcpdump -nn -l -c 100 -i en0 'dst port 53' 2> /dev/null | grep -Eo '[A-Z0-9]+\? [^ ]+' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
     14 A? api.github.com.
     14 AAAA? api.github.com.
      9 HTTPS? www.apple.com.
      6 A? gateway.icloud.com.
      3 PTR? 50.1.168.192.in-addr.arpa.

blocks.text: Seeing both `A?` and `AAAA?` for one name is normal: the resolver asks for IPv4 and IPv6 addresses together. `PTR?` lines are reverse lookups, such as the reverse name of `192.168.1.50`.
**Live filter with grep.** `grep` on a live stream needs `--line-buffered` or its own output block-buffers when writing to a pipe:

blocks.code: sudo tcpdump -nn -l -i en0 | grep --line-buffered 'Flags \[S\]' | head -5

blocks.text: **Handshake round trip from a saved capture.** `-tt` prints epoch seconds, so awk can subtract the time of the first SYN from the time of the first SYN+ACK:

blocks.code:
tcpdump -nn -tt -r trace.pcap 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0' 2> /dev/null \
  | awk '/Flags \[S\],/ && !t0 {t0 = $1} /Flags \[S\.\],/ && t0 {printf "%.1f ms\n", ($1 - t0) * 1000; exit}'

blocks.text: The first pattern remembers the time of the first plain SYN (`[S]`); the second fires on the first SYN+ACK (`[S.]`), prints the difference in milliseconds and exits. It measures one connection. For a file with many connections, key the times by the port pair.
Common mistakes

items.text: **Capturing without `-n`.** tcpdump does reverse DNS for every address, which generates DNS traffic that appears in your own capture.
**Capturing on the wrong interface.** If your Wi-Fi is `en0` and you capture on `en1`, you get silence. Check `route -n get default`.
**Forgetting the quotes.** `tcp[tcpflags]` and anything with `(` or `&` must be quoted in zsh.
**A display filter used as a capture filter** (or the reverse). `ip.addr == x` is Wireshark; `host x` is BPF.
**No `-c` on a long capture.** Disk fills and the terminal drowns. Always bound a capture.
**Root-owned pcap.** Files written with `sudo` need `sudo chown $USER file` before a normal user can open them.
**Capturing over the SSH session you are logged into.** Exclude port 22 or you create a feedback loop.
**Sharing a pcap.** Cookies, tokens and passwords in plain-text protocols are in it. Read it before you send it anywhere.
**Expecting to read HTTPS bodies.** You will not. Capture shows the metadata, not the encrypted payload.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Watch a handshake you caused

task.text: On your own Mac, start `python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1`, then capture 12 packets on `lo0` for `tcp port 8000` while you run `curl -s -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:8000/`. In the output, find the three handshake packets by their flags, and the packet that carries the HTTP request.

hints: The interface for loopback is `lo0`. Do not forget `sudo`, `-nn` and a quoted filter.
The handshake is `[S]`, `[S.]` and `[.]`. The request is the first `[P.]` from the client port.
blocks.solution:
sudo tcpdump -nn -i lo0 -c 12 'tcp port 8000'
curl -s -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:8000/

why.text: The three flags `S`, `S.` and `.` are the SYN, SYN+ACK and ACK of the handshake. The first `P.` from the ephemeral port carries the request; its `length` equals the size of the HTTP request text. The server's FIN arrives first because `http.server` speaks HTTP/1.0 and closes after each response.

blocks.title: Save, then analyze without root

task.text: Capture 100 packets of anything on your active interface into `trace.pcap`, take ownership of the file, and then, without `sudo`, answer: how many packets does it hold, and which five IP addresses appear most often?

hints: `-w` writes the file; `-r` reads it. `sudo chown $USER trace.pcap` fixes ownership.
With `-q` the destination is the fifth field and ends with a colon.
blocks.solution:
sudo tcpdump -nn -i en0 -c 100 -w trace.pcap
sudo chown $USER trace.pcap
tcpdump -nn -r trace.pcap 2> /dev/null | wc -l
tcpdump -nn -q -r trace.pcap 'ip' 2> /dev/null | awk '{print $3; print $5}' | sed 's/\.[0-9]*:*$//' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5

why.text: Capturing needs root, but reading a file does not. Both source and destination are counted so you see every address, yours included. The `sed` strips the trailing port.

blocks.title: Which names did I look up?

task.text: Capture UDP port 53 traffic going out from your Mac while you run `dig example.com` and `dig python.org`. Print only the query names and types, one per line, without duplicates.

hints: Queries go to port 53, so `dst port 53` shows queries and not answers.
A query line contains `A? name.`; `grep -Eo` can extract it.
blocks.solution: sudo tcpdump -nn -l -c 20 -i en0 'dst port 53' 2> /dev/null | grep -Eo '[A-Z0-9]+\? [^ ]+' | sort -u

why.text: The filter keeps only queries, the regex extracts the question token, and `sort -u` removes repeats. Other applications also query DNS while you capture, so unrelated names may appear.

blocks.title: Annotate a trace

task.text: Below is the capture from the DNS-then-HTTP section, with the middle lines removed. Answer from the lines alone:

items.text: Which packet is the first to carry data from the client, and how many bytes?
What is the round-trip time to the web server, measured from the handshake?
How long did the DNS lookup take?
Who closes the connection first in the full trace below?
The server's SYN+ACK advertises `mss 1380`. What does it limit?

hints: The handshake round trip is the time between the SYN and the SYN+ACK.
A FIN consumes one sequence number, so the final ACK is one higher than the FIN's `seq`.
blocks.solution:
1. The `[P.]` with seq 1:75, 74 bytes: the HTTP GET request.
2. About 19.3 ms (31.990 minus 12.650).
3. About 11.8 ms (the answer arrives at .011840).
4. The client: its [F.] at .064100 comes before the server's at .083500.
5. The largest TCP segment the client may send to the server (1380 bytes of payload); the client's own MSS (1460) limits what the server sends. The 1448-byte segment is 1460 minus 12 bytes of timestamp option.

why.text: Every answer comes from a handful of rules: flags show the phase, `seq a:b` gives the payload size, timestamps give delays, and `ack` numbers prove what was received. After enough traces these become instantly readable.

blocks.title: Break it on purpose, then fix it

task.text: Run each command, read the failure, and repair it:

items.text: `tcpdump -nn -i lo0 -c 3 tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0`
`tcpdump -nn -i lo0 -c 3 'tcp port 8000'` (as a normal user)
`sudo tcpdump -nn -i en9 -c 3`
`sudo tcpdump -nn -r trace.pcap 'port 53 and'`

hints: The first one fails in zsh before tcpdump starts. The third names an interface that does not exist; `-D` lists real ones.
blocks.solution:
sudo tcpdump -nn -i lo0 -c 3 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0'
sudo tcpdump -nn -i lo0 -c 3 'tcp port 8000'
sudo tcpdump -D
sudo tcpdump -nn -r trace.pcap 'port 53 and port 53'

why.text: (1) zsh treats `[` and `&` specially, so the filter must be one quoted string, and it needs `sudo` too. (2) Without root, tcpdump cannot open the BPF device and says permission denied. (3) `-D` shows which interfaces exist. (4) A filter that ends in `and` is a syntax error; compile errors appear immediately, before any packet is read.

blocks.title: From pcap to a ranked list with tshark

task.text: Install Wireshark's command-line tools (`brew install --cask wireshark-app`), capture 200 packets while you browse a few sites, and then list the TLS server names your Mac connected to, most frequent first.

hints: A ClientHello is `tls.handshake.type == 1`, and the field is `tls.handshake.extensions_server_name`.
Use `-T fields -e` and pipe to `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn`.
blocks.solution:
sudo tshark -i en0 -f 'tcp port 443' -c 200 -w tls.pcap
sudo chown $USER tls.pcap
tshark -r tls.pcap -Y 'tls.handshake.type == 1' -T fields -e tls.handshake.extensions_server_name | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

why.text: The capture filter keeps the file small, the display filter keeps only ClientHello messages, and the field extractor prints the plain-text server name. `uniq -c` needs sorted input, so `sort` comes first.

questions.q: Why does tcpdump usually need `sudo` on macOS?

options.text: It must edit the routing table
It opens the BPF devices, which only root can open by default
Packets are encrypted for normal users

questions.why: Capture reads copies of frames from `/dev/bpf*`, which are root-only unless a helper such as ChmodBPF changes the permissions.

questions.q: In a tcpdump line, what does `Flags [S.]` mean?

options.text: SYN only: a client opening a connection
SYN plus ACK: a server accepting a connection

questions.why: The letter is the flag and a trailing dot means ACK is also set. `[S]` opens, `[S.]` accepts, `[.]` acknowledges.

questions.q: Which of these is a Wireshark display filter, not a BPF capture filter?
questions.why: Dotted field names such as `ip.addr` and `tcp.flags.syn` are display-filter syntax. BPF uses keywords such as `host`, `net` and `port`.

questions.q: You run `sudo tcpdump -nn -i en0 tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0` and zsh says `no matches found`. What is the fix?

options.text: Put the whole filter in single quotes

questions.why: zsh expands the brackets as a glob before tcpdump runs. One quoted string reaches tcpdump unchanged.

questions.q: A capture shows `Flags [S]` from your Mac to a server, followed 30 seconds later by another `[S]` and no reply. What does this suggest?

options.text: The server refused the connection with a reset
The SYN is being dropped or ignored, so something in the path is filtering or the host is down

questions.why: A closed port answers at once with `[R.]`. Repeated SYNs with no answer at all mean the packets are silently dropped, a firewall or a dead host.

questions.q: Which tshark option prints only the fields you name?
questions.why: `-T fields` changes the output format, and each `-e` names a field. The result is tab-separated and pipes cleanly.

blocks.title: trace-url, capture one request end to end

blocks.text: Build `trace-url.zsh`: it resolves a host, captures only the packets of one `curl` request (DNS plus the web connection), saves them, and prints a summary of the handshake and DNS timing. It only records traffic that your own command generates, filtered to one address and port 53.
Step 1: Capture by hand
Run each piece yourself first so you know what the script must do:

blocks.code:
ip=$(dig +short example.com | grep -E '^[0-9.]+$' | head -1)
sudo tcpdump -nn -U -i en0 -w one.pcap "host $ip or port 53" &
sleep 1; curl -s -o /dev/null http://example.com; sleep 1
sudo kill -INT $!

blocks.text: The `&` puts tcpdump in the background, the first `sleep` gives it time to start listening, and `kill -INT` is Control-C, which makes tcpdump close the file properly.
Step 2: Summarize

blocks.code:
tcpdump -nn -tt -r one.pcap 2> /dev/null | head -20
tcpdump -nn -tt -r one.pcap 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0' 2> /dev/null

blocks.text: Step 3: The script

blocks.code:
#!/bin/zsh
# Usage: ./trace-url.zsh example.com
# Captures DNS plus the traffic to this host while curl fetches http://HOST/
# Only your own request is recorded: the filter allows one IP and port 53.
setopt pipefail

host=${1:?usage: trace-url.zsh HOST}
iface=$(route -n get default 2> /dev/null | awk '/interface:/ {print $2}')
ip=$(dig +short "$host" | grep -E '^[0-9.]+$' | head -1)
[[ -n $iface && -n $ip ]] || { print -u2 "cannot find interface or address"; exit 1; }

pcap=trace-${host}-$(date +%H%M%S).pcap
print "interface $iface, server $ip, writing $pcap"

sudo -v || exit 1
sudo tcpdump -nn -U -i $iface -w $pcap "host $ip or port 53" 2> /dev/null &
cap=$!
trap 'sudo kill -INT $cap 2> /dev/null' EXIT
sleep 1

curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'curl: %{http_code} in %{time_total}s\n' "http://$host/"
sleep 1
sudo kill -INT $cap 2> /dev/null; wait $cap 2> /dev/null
trap - EXIT
sudo chown $USER $pcap

echo; echo "== packets: $(tcpdump -nn -r $pcap 2> /dev/null | wc -l | tr -d ' ')"
echo "== DNS"
tcpdump -nn -r $pcap 'port 53' 2> /dev/null | cut -c1-110
echo "== handshake"
tcpdump -nn -tt -r $pcap 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0' 2> /dev/null \
  | awk '/Flags \[S\],/ && !t0 {t0 = $1} /Flags \[S\.\],/ && t0 && !done {printf "SYN to SYN+ACK: %.1f ms\n", ($1 - t0) * 1000; done = 1}'
chmod +x trace-url.zsh && ./trace-url.zsh example.com

blocks.text: Step 4: Open it in Wireshark

Double-click the pcap. Right-click the first TCP packet and choose Follow, TCP Stream to read the HTTP exchange. Then try the display filter `tcp.analysis.retransmission` (it is empty on a healthy connection) and Statistics, Conversations.

Add an option for a port other than 80 (and use `tshark -z follow,tcp,ascii,0` to print the stream). Print the time from the `[P.]` request to the first `[P.]` response, which is the server wait. Compare the numbers with `curl -w '%{time_connect} %{time_starttransfer}'` and explain any difference.
Try it in the practice terminal

The simulator cannot capture packets, but it has the lab files, and the filters and pipelines in this chapter are ordinary text processing. Practice the parts that do not need a capture: reading `ping.log` and `scan.txt` is the same skill as reading a pcap summary.
Glossary and next steps
Next: [Remote Access with SSH](#ssh) takes you from watching packets to controlling machines across them, with keys, config files and tunnels.

terms.def: The standard file format for captured packets, read by tcpdump, Wireshark and tshark
Berkeley Packet Filter: the in-kernel filter language and mechanism used for capture filters
A BPF expression that decides which packets are recorded
A Wireshark expression that decides which already-captured packets are shown
A capture mode in which an interface accepts frames addressed to other hosts; on switched or Wi-Fi networks you still see little
Maximum bytes captured per packet; modern tools default to the whole packet
TCP flag that opens a connection (synchronize sequence numbers)
TCP flag that aborts or refuses a connection
Counter of bytes in a TCP stream, used to order data and acknowledge it
Address Resolution Protocol: asks "who has this IP?" on the local network to learn the MAC address
The server name sent in clear text in a TLS ClientHello
The Wireshark helper that lets an admin account read the BPF devices without sudo
Wireshark's command-line analyzer, able to print chosen fields for use in pipes
Apple's virtual capture interface that tags each packet with its process name
